questions.learningObjective: Explain how a narrator's retrospective account of his own making is built.
questions.stem: The programming notes for a new archive ask how a novel presents the making of its narrator, so explain how the account of his own formation is constructed.

answer.exemplar: The narrator is not a child writing as he happens but a man looking back who knows how the story ends and has caught the errors of his own earlier judgement. He reports his early contempt for the man who found him, his dreams of gentility, and the disappointment that follows each expectation, and then revises the meanings he once attached to them, so the account of his making is also an account of his own reading being corrected.

questions.explanation: The narrator knows the outcome and re-reads his earlier self accordingly, so his account corrects its own first judgements. Reading it as a straightforward childhood memoir misses the layers of revision.
questions.hint: The narrator looks back on his own mistakes.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how the meaning of a novel's title is reversed across it.

answer.exemplar: At first the phrase means the social advancement the boy is promised by a fortune he does not yet know the source of, and everything in the first half is organised around the hope of gentility. By the end the same words mean the moral expectations he sets himself, the habits and company he has chosen, and the question of what kind of man he has made of himself. The same two words thus carry a worldly hope at one end of the story and a moral standard at the other.

questions.explanation: The title first names what the boy expects to receive and later names what he must become, so the book's argument about money turns into a book about character. Reading the title as a single fixed meaning misses the reversal.
questions.hint: The words stay the same; the sense turns over.

answer.exemplar: The label means that the story is delivered through the records people leave behind: letters, wills, account books, official reports and sworn statements, each reproduced in the text rather than summarised in a narrator's voice. It gives the reader something to inspect, so the mystery becomes a matter of reading evidence rather than of trusting a teller, and it enforces distrust of every witness, since each document is partial and interested, and no single paper can be the whole truth.

questions.explanation: The label points to a narration built from reproducible records, which makes the reader an examiner of evidence and guarantees that every source is partial. Reading it as a general realist manner misses what the documentary form is for.

answer.exemplar: Knowing the outcome lets the narrator hold two accounts of the same moment at once, the boy's eager expectation and the man's later understanding of it, and the writing moves by placing them side by side so that the reader watches an expectation being made and then being tested. answer.exemplar: One half of the book shows a court that cannot finish its business, where a case drags on because the law cannot even establish who is dead, and the other shows what law costs the people caught inside it. Placed together, the two narratives say that the law is not merely slow but damaging, and that the harm is not confined to the parties: it spreads through households, through servants, and through the children who grow up inside it. questions.stem: A heritage strategy asks what a novelist gained by making his industrial town a general type rather than a named place, so explain the point of the exercise.

answer.exemplar: By making the town a type, the novelist can argue about a whole way of organising towns, not one instance of it, and he can do so with a rigour a single case would not allow, since nothing in the place is too particular to be argued with. The uniformity of the town is itself the argument: one industry, one owner, one measure of worth, and every voice pitched to the same key, so that the reader sees a system rather than a collection of characters. The town's namelessness is what makes it possible to be exact.

questions.explanation: Generalising the town lets the novel argue about a whole type of place with precision, and the uniformity of the place is the argument itself. Reading the exercise as vagueness or as simple realism misses the rigour it makes possible.

answer.exemplar: The novel shows the apparatus of gentility, the coat, the visiting card, the leg, the gloves, and shows it being tried on and found hollow, so that a boy measures his worth against a costume rather than a self. Because the boy comes from a labouring family and is a pupil of a school that forbids imagination, his class position and his ignorance are given as the ground of his mistake, and the book's final argument becomes about what he must unlearn before he can be told who he is.

questions.explanation: The novel's most quoted figures of dress and manner are used to show gentility as a surface that can be bought and worn. Reading them as social fact, as satire of manners for its own sake, or as evidence of bad taste misses what they are used to show.
questions.hint: Look at what he is measured by, and by what.

It conceals the subject, so the reader must work out where the story is really set

questions.explanation: Naming the town in the title makes the place the book's true subject, and the people within it are examined as its residents rather than as the novel's hero. Reading the title as reference, concealment, or series marker misses the deliberate emphasis it carries.
